title: Based vs native rollups
intro: Who should put a rollup's transactions in order, and who should check that its results are right? Ethereum researchers and rollup builders have argued over two answers: let Ethereum's own block proposers do the sequencing (based rollups), or let Ethereum's own execution do the checking through a built-in tool (native rollups, EIP-8079). Underneath sits a bigger question, how much of a layer 2 Ethereum should take on, and the people who build layer 2s have a say in it.

stops.author: JustinDrake
stops.note: The proposal itself, in its author's words: what a based rollup is, why it would be simple and aligned with L1, and the costs he names himself. The map opens here (Alex, 7 Nov 2026).

lines.text: We highlight a special subset of rollups we call "based" or "L1-sequenced". The sequencing of such rollups—based sequencing—is maximally simple and inherits L1 liveness and decentralisation. Moreover, based rollups are particularly economically aligned with their base L1.

A rollup is said to be based, or L1-sequenced, when its sequencing is driven by the base L1. More concretely, a based rollup is one where the next L1 proposer may, in collaboration with L1 searchers and builders, permissionlessly include the next rollup block as part of the next L1 block.
Based rollups forgo MEV to the L1, limiting their revenue to base fees. Counter-intuitively, this may increase overall income for based rollups.

Fast pre-confirmations are trivial with centralised sequencing, and achievable with an external PoS consensus. Fast pre-confirmations with L1 sequencing is an open problem with promising research avenues including EigenLayer, inclusion lists, and builder bonds.

stops.author: bruno_f
stops.note: The first sharp reply on the same thread: liveness can be recovered without L1 sequencing, and latency is the real cost.

lines.text: If there's a liveness failure, rollups can recover by having a new set of sequencers (or even just one) be chosen on L1. There's no reason to stop the chain and force people to do a mass exit. We can always find new people to continue building blocks.

Regarding the disadvantages, latency is a big one. With L2 sequencers you can have L2 block finality in 1s which, while much weaker than L1 block finality for sure, still provides a decent guarantee for most use cases.

stops.author: JustinDrake
stops.note: The answer to the latency objection: let L1 proposers promise fast, slashable preconfirmations.

lines.text: Based preconfs offer a competitive user experience for based sequencing, with latencies on the order of 100ms.

A transaction with a preconf promise from the next preconfer can be immediately included and executed onchain by any proposer ahead of that preconfer. The preconfer is then expected to honour any remaining promises on their slot using the inclusion list.

stops.author: ben-a-fisch
stops.note: A shared-sequencer view of based preconfs: a weaker guarantee than finality, and a question about how much stake backs it.

lines.text: This seems to offer a different (weaker) type of "preconfirmation" guarantee than *finality,* which is what a consensus protocol like Espresso's Hotshot protocol provides. What happens to these preconfs when there is a reorg on Ethereum's LMD Ghost protocol? Also, how much stake would be slashed for invalid preconfirmations in this proposal versus a protocol like the Espresso Sequencer (e.g., assuming the same amount of L1 validator stake is participating in each via Eigenlayer)? For the Espresso Sequencer the amount slashed would be 1/3 of the entire stake.

stops.author: Lin Oshitani
stops.note: A based-rollup builder names a cost of the fast path: naive based preconfs push externalities back onto L1 and its searchers.

lines.text: However, compared to non-preconfirming based sequencing, naive implementations of based preconfirmations introduce negative externalities that require thoughtful consideration.

Given that L2 transaction fees are typically low, searchers may choose to avoid latency races altogether and instead flood the rollup with probabilistic arbitrage attempts. This can be done by spamming an arbitrage contract that attempts an arbitrage and rollbacks if it fails.

stops.author: JustinDrake
stops.note: The native rollups proposal in its author's words: the second half of the debate starts here, and the post says based and native are separate choices.

lines.text: This post suggests a pathway for EVM-equivalent rollups to rid themselves of security councils and other attack vectors, unlocking full Ethereum L1 security.

Based rollups and native rollups are orthogonal concepts: "based" relates to L1 sequencing whereas "native" relates to L1 execution. A rollup that is simultaneously based and native is whimsically called an "ultra sound rollup".

Today's EVM-equivalent optimistic and zk-rollups have thousands of lines of code for their fraud proof game or SNARK verifier that could collapse to a single line of code. Native rollups also don't require ancillary infrastructure like proving networks, watchtowers, and security councils.

stops.author: edfelten
stops.note: The first L2-side objection: real rollups differ from L1 in ways the state transition function must carry.

lines.text: A word of caution here. Practical L2 designs have several features that don't seem compatible with the design described here.

L2s do gas accounting differently than L1 does, for example by adding a surcharge to pay for data availability; or if the L2 has variable block time for efficiency, then adjusting gas prices based on timestamp rather than block number. Doing this trustlessly requires changes to the state transition function.

stops.title: Still a draft
stops.body: Native rollups are written up as EIP-8079, which would expose Ethereum's state transition function through a new EXECUTE precompile. It is a Draft, created 13 November 2025, and no fork has proposed or scheduled it. The EIP leaves sequencing open, so a native rollup can be based or not. EIP-8025, the optional execution proofs that Gajinder Singh expects to enable native rollup experiments, was declined for Hegota at All Core Devs Consensus #189 on 15 October 2026 (Forkcast). The Strawmap on strawmap.org, updated 2 November 2026, places native rollups in the placeholder fork L*.
stops.note: Primary sources: EIP-8079 (eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8079): status Draft, created 13 Nov 2025, authors Luca Donno and Justin Drake, abstract "Expose the state transition function to the execution layer via a new EXECUTE precompile"; its Rationale says a native rollup can use a permissioned sequencer, based sequencing, or a staked network. Forkcast EIP record (ethereum/forkcast src/data/eips/8079.json): empty forkRelationships. The only All Core Devs decisions found on this map concern EIP-7917 (CFI #155, SFI #158, live in Fusaka), a preconfirmation fix; none decides based versus native. EIP-8025: Forkcast record, Proposed for Hegota at ACDC #178 (14 May 2026), Declined at ACDC #189 (15 Oct 2026). strawmap.org drawing read 10 Nov 2026 ('updated Nov 2, 2026'): native rollups at L*, mandatory proofs at K*. Re-read 10 Nov 2026: EIP-8079 still Draft (last change 21 Nov 2025, formatting), Forkcast record still has no fork relationships.
